title: Bridging a care gap under sustained threat: A forward psychological support capability for acute stress reactions in combat.
abstract: Acute stress reactions (ASR) frequently emerge during combat operations and can rapidly impair attention, decision-making, leadership, and unit functioning. Although peer-based stabilization protocols provide an important first-line response, situations may arise in which symptoms exceed the capacity of peer responders while evacuation is neither feasible nor operationally desirable. This creates a critical operational gap in managing performance-impairing acute stress in forward combat environments. The present Brief Report introduces Combat-Adapted Psychological First Aid (CA-PFA), a frontline psychological support capability designed to restore functional performance under sustained threat. CA-PFA adapts core elements of Psychological First Aid to combat conditions and emphasizes rapid stabilization, cognitive clarification, reinforcement of functional identity, and return to operational engagement. Two illustrative cases from forward operational zones are presented to demonstrate the clinical indications, intervention components, and immediate operational outcomes associated with CA-PFA. In both cases, brief interventions delivered near the point of combat exposure were followed by observable improvements in functional control and operational engagement without evacuation. These examples illustrate the feasibility of embedding a forward psychological support tier within stepped-care responses to acute stress reactions. By focusing on rapid restoration of functional performance rather than distress reduction alone, CA-PFA may provide a practical approach for managing acute stress reactions in high-threat operational environments. Further empirical research is needed to evaluate its effectiveness, scalability, and potential role within broader military stress-management systems.
